messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 71

**Clinical Vignette: “Colonel Mark” (age 56, combat pilot)**

Mark is a retired colonel who flew F-16s for twenty-two years. He still speaks about flying with a quiet precision—the way he describes the weight of the throttle, the shift of G-forces, the smell of jet fuel on his flight suit—as though he’s giving a briefing. But when he talks about the accident, his voice thins. He pauses. He checks the corners of the room.

The accident happened five years ago, during a routine training sortie over the desert. He was on a low-level navigation run, pushing through a canyon at four hundred knots. A bird strike shattered the canopy. The Plexiglas imploded into the cockpit, and a piece—he thinks it was a piece—sliced his left arm above the elbow before lodging in his side. He remembers the blood spreading across his flight suit like a map of somewhere else. He remembers the calm, automated voice of the warning system: *Terrain, terrain. Pull up.* He pulled. The jet screamed. He blacked out from the G-load on the way up.

He woke at the base hospital. He had a collapsed lung, a fractured humerus, and twenty-seven stitches across his ribs. The bird—a vulture, they told him—was destroyed. The aircraft was repaired. He was grounded for six months. He never took that same canyon route again.

Now, five years later, Mark is still retired. He sits in his home office with a model of an F-16 on his desk, but he rarely touches it. His wife, Sarah, has asked him to take it down. He can’t explain why he keeps it—maybe it’s a marker, a reminder of who he used to be. He doesn’t fly anymore. He doesn’t even drive on the highway if he can avoid it. Last winter, a friend offered him a ride in a Cessna. Mark’s hands started shaking before they reached the runway. He said no.

He has nightmares most nights. The dream isn’t the crash itself—it’s the moment before, the split-second when he knew something was wrong but couldn’t react. He wakes with his heart pounding, convinced the ceiling is dropping toward him. Sarah has learned not to touch him when he first wakes. He’s snapped at her too many times. Once, he threw a lamp across the bedroom. He doesn’t remember doing it, but she told him afterward. He felt a thick, crawling shame for days.

During the day, Mark is watchful. He scans parking lots for abandoned cars. He avoids crowded restaurants and refuses to sit with his back to the door. At the grocery store, if someone walks too close behind him, he freezes, his shoulders tightening. He doesn’t call it hypervigilance. He calls it “being smart for a man my age.”

He has tried to tell Sarah what he feels, but the words scatter. He can describe the mechanics of an aircraft engine with clinical clarity, but the internal pressure—the feeling that something is about to go wrong, that the world is a thin film over something terrible—eludes language. So he stays quiet. He spends hours in the garage, arranging tools, never fixing anything. He can’t concentrate on a book. He worries that he’s becoming someone else, someone brittle and quick to anger.

He avoids photographs of himself in uniform. He avoids old squadron reunions. He avoids the smell of grilled meat because it reminds him of the field hospital. He doesn’t know why. He just knows the smell makes his chest tighten.

He came to therapy because Sarah said she couldn’t live with the version of him that sleeps one hour a night and flinches at every car backfire. He sat in the chair across from me, hands resting on his knees, back perfectly straight. He said, “I don’t know if this will help.” But he’s still coming. Every Tuesday at 10 a.m. He arrives twenty minutes early. He always checks the parking lot before he walks in.
